title: Making Your Own: Fresh Similes
tagline: patterns, extended and epic similes, and new life for old clichés
why: Advanced speakers don't only recognise similes; they make them. Knowing the grammar patterns behind similes lets you create fresh, precise comparisons for stories, presentations and writing, and avoid the tired ones.
understand: simile compares, metaphor says one thing is another
able: build your own similes with five different grammar patterns
develop a simple comparison into an extended simile in speech or writing
refresh a cliché by twisting, extending or contradicting it
mistakes: The office was as quiet like a library.
As quiet as a library. The as ... as frame needs the second as.
She sang as a bird at the wedding.
She sang like a bird. As a bird means in the role of a bird.
He looked at me like I was a ghost, in his report to the board.
In formal writing, prefer as if I were a ghost. Like + clause is fine in casual speech.
The hall was more quiet as a church.
The hall was quieter than a church. Comparatives take than.
Just as the river carves the valley, also patience shapes a career.
Just as ..., so patience shapes a career. The epic pattern is just as ... so ....
bigidea: A simile compares two unlike things openly, with a signal word: like, as, as if, the way, than. A metaphor drops the signal and says one thing is another. A simile is a little more modest and more precise: it says in this one way, these two things are alike.

A simile becomes a cliché when the second half is completely predictable: if you say as busy as a ..., everyone thinks bee. A fresh simile is concrete, specific and slightly surprising, but instantly clear: as busy as a phone charger at an airport. The test is simple: can the listener picture it, and did they not see it coming?

Similes can also grow. An extended simile develops one comparison over several clauses. An epic or Homeric simile, named after the Greek poet Homer, turns the comparison into a small scene of its own, often in the pattern just as ..., so .... You'll hear shorter versions in speeches, sermons and sports commentary.
hidden: The traffic this morning was like a parking lot.
He talks to his car as if it were a person.
She's as stubborn as a mule, just like her mother.
Their new house is bigger than a hotel.
The kids ran off like a shot when the bell rang.
It feels as though summer lasted a week.

expressions.meaning: compares one quality to something that has a lot of it
expressions.example: After the funeral the house was as quiet as a held breath.
expressions.bend: Negative: not as tidy as a hotel. Intensified: just as, twice as. Casual speech drops the first as: quiet as a mouse.
expressions.note: The easiest pattern to refresh: keep the adjective, change the noun. Trap: never as ... like.

expressions.meaning: compares an action or a thing to a picture
expressions.example: The rumour went through the office like a cold through a daycare.
expressions.bend: After almost any verb: run like, look like, spread like. Add detail to make it fresh: like a cold through a daycare rather than like wildfire.
expressions.note: Like + noun compares; as + noun gives a role (she worked as a nurse). This is the most common source of simile errors.

expressions.example: He shook my hand as if he were signing a peace treaty.
expressions.bend: Formal: as if he were; everyday: as if he was; casual North American: like he was.
expressions.note: As if and as though mean the same. Use the past tense (or were) for something unreal; the present for something possibly true: it looks as if it's going to rain.

expressions.meaning: compares how two actions are done
expressions.example: She carried the folder the way you'd carry a newborn baby.
expressions.bend: Often with you or someone: the way you'd ..., the way a cat watches a bird. The way that is possible but heavier.
expressions.note: A quiet, elegant pattern favoured by novelists. It compares manner, so it suits actions and gestures better than qualities.

expressions.meaning: compares by saying something goes beyond a familiar extreme
expressions.example: That budget meeting was more painful than a root canal.
expressions.bend: Comparative adjectives: quieter than a library, colder than a landlord's heart; also less ... than.
expressions.note: Only a simile when the things are unlike: taller than his brother is just a comparison. Often humorous exaggeration.

expressions.meaning: a simile developed over several clauses or sentences
expressions.example: Starting a business is like planting an orchard: you dig, you water, you wait for years, and one late frost can take the lot.
expressions.bend: Usually starts with a short simile, then adds a colon or you ... you ... to develop it. Keep every detail inside the same picture.
expressions.note: Powerful in presentations and speeches. Trap: switching to a new image halfway creates a mixed metaphor.

expressions.meaning: a long, detailed comparison that becomes a small scene of its own
expressions.example: Just as a farmer watches the sky all week for hail, so the finance minister watched the markets before the budget.
expressions.bend: Pattern: just as ..., so ... or like ..., so .... Can run to several sentences in literature.
expressions.note: Named after Homer's Iliad and Odyssey. In modern use it sounds grand, so it suits speeches, eulogies or deliberate humour.

expressions.meaning: refreshing an old simile by twisting, extending or contradicting it
expressions.example: My uncle isn't just stubborn as a mule; he's as stubborn as a mule with a lawyer.
expressions.bend: Extend it (a mule with a lawyer), swap the noun (as busy as a bee in a flower shop), or deny it (far from cool as a cucumber, he was a pickle in a heatwave).
expressions.note: Native listeners enjoy the surprise because they know the original. Do it once per conversation; more sounds like showing off.

culture.how: Homer's war epic is full of long similes that pause the battle to show a scene from ordinary life: warriors like lions attacking a flock, armies like waves. In one famous passage, the warrior Glaucus compares the generations of men to the leaves of a tree, which fall and grow again each spring.
culture.ask: Glaucus compares human generations to leaves. What image would you use for generations in your family?
culture.find: Iliad epic simile Glaucus generations of leaves Book 6

culture.work: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
culture.how: Eliot's poem opens with one of the most startling similes in modern poetry: the evening sky is compared not to something beautiful but to a hospital patient lying unconscious on an operating table. Readers expecting a romantic sunset get something cold and clinical instead, and that shock sets the nervous, uneasy mood of the whole poem.
culture.ask: Describe a sunset, a city street or a Monday morning with a simile that surprises the listener instead of the one they expect.
culture.find: T. S. Eliot Prufrock opening simile evening patient etherised

culture.work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud
culture.how: The title itself is a simile: the speaker compares himself, walking alone, to a single cloud drifting over hills and valleys, until he comes across a crowd of daffodils by a lake. The simile sets the mood of solitude that the flowers then break. Compare Langston Hughes's Harlem, a whole poem built from similes.
culture.ask: Make a simile for how you feel when you walk alone somewhere you love.
culture.find: Wordsworth I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud daffodils

culture.how: The title simile compares the feeling of hearing someone's voice, and of being close to them, to the experience of prayer. By borrowing religious language for love, Madonna made an ordinary pop comparison feel bold, and the song and its video caused a major controversy when they came out.
culture.ask: What would you compare a powerful experience, like falling in love or hearing great news, to? Try a fresh image from an unexpected area of life.

match.why: As quiet as a held breath: one quality, quietness.

match.r: compares an action or thing to a picture
match.why: The rumour spread like a cold through a daycare.
As if he were signing a treaty: he wasn't really.

match.r: compares the manner of two actions
match.why: She held it the way you'd hold a baby: how she held it.
More painful than a root canal: comic exaggeration.

match.r: one comparison developed over several clauses
match.why: Starting a business is like planting an orchard: you dig, you water, you wait...

match.r: a comparison that becomes a small scene
match.why: Named after Homer. Pattern: just as ..., so ...

match.r: twisting an old simile to make it new
match.why: As stubborn as a mule with a lawyer.

sort.h: Sort the examples: is each a cliché simile, a fresh simile, or a metaphor (no comparison word)?

items.why: Everyone can finish it: a cliché.
Common cliché for someone pale with fear.

items.w: as busy as a phone charger at an airport
items.why: Specific, surprising and easy to picture: fresh.

items.w: he slept like a cat on a radiator
items.why: A fresh twist: warm, deep, contented sleep.

items.w: she smiled the way you smile at a parking ticket
as cold as a hockey rink at 6 a.m.

items.why: No like or as: it says time is a thief.
A metaphor; the simile would be like daggers.

pick.q: My office chair squeaks ___ it's in pain.
pick.why: An imagined situation + clause = as if (or as though).

pick.q: She read the contract ___ a detective reads a crime scene.
pick.why: Comparing the manner of two actions + clause = the way.

pick.q: My teenage son is ___ than a hibernating bear on weekends.
Which simile is the freshest way to describe a crowded subway? It was ___.
opts: as packed as a fridge after Thanksgiving
pick.why: Packed like sardines and busy as a beehive are clichés; the Thanksgiving fridge is specific and surprising.

pick.q: In a eulogy: ___ an old maple shelters the whole yard, so she sheltered all of us.
pick.why: The epic simile pattern: just as ..., so ...

pick.q: The new manager is ___ a hawk; nothing escapes her.
pick.why: Like + noun compares. As a hawk would mean in the role of a hawk.

opts: The economy is like a bicycle: stop pedalling and it falls over.
The economy is as bad as ever.
pick.why: An extended simile develops the comparison. The second is a metaphor; the third isn't a simile.

pick.q: Which version turns the cliché? He's not just as old as the hills; he's ___.
opts: old enough to remember when the hills were delivered
pick.why: Twisting the cliché into a surprising picture refreshes it. Repeating it, or garbling it, doesn't.

spot.q: Our new apartment is as small like a shoebox.
spot.why: The frame is as + adjective + as.

spot.q: My grandmother can still dance as a teenager at a wedding.
spot.why: Like compares. As a teenager means when she was a teenager.

spot.q: The lake was more calm as a mirror this morning.
spot.why: Comparatives take than: calmer than a mirror.

spot.q: Just as the tide returns twice a day, also the voters come back to their old party.
spot.why: The epic pattern is just as ..., so ...

spot.q: She guarded the recipe the way a dragon guarding its gold.
opts: a dragon to guard its gold
spot.why: The way needs a full clause with a finite verb: the way a dragon guards its gold.

type.q: The house was as silent ___ a closed museum.
type.why: As + adjective + as: the second as is needed.

type.q: He spent money ___ it grew on trees.
type.why: As if or as though + clause; like is casual.

type.q: The traffic moved ___ a glacier with a headache.
type.why: Like + noun: a fresh simile for very slow traffic.

type.q: She checked her phone the ___ a gambler checks a slot machine.
type.why: The way + clause compares the manner of two actions.

type.q: The motel room was smaller ___ a ferry cabin.
Just as a good coach knows when to rest a player, ___ a good leader knows when to step back.
type.why: Epic simile pattern: just as ..., so ...

bend.q: In a formal report about an unexpected market crash: ___
opts: Investors reacted as if the bank were already insolvent.
Investors reacted like the bank was already insolvent, you know.
Investors reacted as the bank were already insolvent.
bend.why: Formal register: as if + were. Like + clause is casual; as alone doesn't introduce an imagined situation.

bend.q: Chatting with a friend about a nervous dog: ___
opts: He's shaking like a leaf in a hairdryer.
He's shaking as like a leaf.
bend.why: Like + noun, extended with a fresh detail: like a leaf in a hairdryer.

bend.q: Writing a short story, you describe a cautious character: ___
opts: She opened the email the way you'd lift the lid off a pot you'd forgotten about.
She opened the email the way of a forgotten pot.
She opened the email as the way of a pot.
bend.why: The way + full clause creates a precise picture of the manner.

bend.q: Refreshing a cliché at a retirement party: ___
opts: Bill isn't as fit as a fiddle; he's as fit as the whole orchestra.
Bill is as fit like a fiddle.
bend.why: Extending the cliché to a whole orchestra makes it fresh and funny. The others are grammar errors.

talk: Wordsworth compared himself to a lonely cloud. Choose a place you love and describe how you feel there with a simile you invent.
Take three clichés: as busy as a bee, sleep like a log, as cold as ice. Turn each one into a fresh simile about your own city or life.
Role-play: you are giving a short toast at a friend's retirement. Include one extended simile and one epic simile with just as ... so ....
Eliot compares an evening sky to a patient on an operating table. Which common simile in English, or in your first language, has become boring, and how could you shock it back to life?
Do you prefer similes or metaphors when you speak? Change one of your fresh similes into a metaphor. Which version is stronger?

match.r: an open comparison using like, as, than or the way
match.why: Her laugh was like a car alarm.
Her laugh was a car alarm.

match.r: a comparison so familiar it's predictable
match.why: As busy as a bee: everyone knows the ending.

match.r: a specific, surprising but clear comparison
match.why: As busy as a phone charger at an airport.
A danger in extended similes: keep to one picture.

match.r: completely dead (cliché played with by Dickens)
match.why: The opening of A Christmas Carol questions it.

pick.q: The printer groaned ___ it were being asked to climb a mountain.
pick.why: An imagined situation + clause = as though (or as if).

pick.q: He tasted the wine ___ a scientist studies a sample.
pick.why: Comparing manner + full clause = the way.

pick.q: Our basement in January is colder ___ a fishing hut on Lake Simcoe.
Which is a metaphor, not a simile? ___
opts: My boss is like a volcano.
My boss erupts like a volcano.
pick.why: No comparison word: my boss is a volcano.

pick.q: Which simile is freshest for a very tidy desk? It was ___.
opts: as neat as a surgeon's tray
pick.why: Neat as a pin is a cliché; a surgeon's tray is specific and vivid.

pick.q: ___ the first robin tells us spring has come, so the first resignation told us the company was changing.
pick.why: Epic simile pattern: just as ..., so ...

spot.q: Her voice was as smooth like warm honey.
spot.why: As + adjective + as: never as ... like.

spot.q: The toddler ate the cake as a vacuum cleaner.
spot.why: Like + noun compares; as + noun means in the role of.

spot.q: The city at night was more bright as a stadium.
He treated his old car the way a collector treating a painting.
opts: of a collector treating a painting
spot.why: The way needs a full clause: the way a collector treats a painting.

type.q: The bread was as hard ___ a hockey puck.
type.why: As + adjective + as: a fresh, Canadian simile.

type.q: My laptop fan sounds ___ a small plane taking off.
They talked about the trip as ___ it had been a military campaign.
He folded the map the ___ a priest folds an altar cloth.
type.why: The way + clause compares the manner of two actions: slowly and with great care.

type.q: The old ferry was slower ___ a canoe paddled by toddlers.
Just as frost brings out the colour of the maples, ___ hardship brings out a person's character.

bank.q: The cat stared at the empty bowl ___ it had been personally insulted.
bank.why: An imagined situation + clause = as if.

bank.q: She held the trophy ___ you'd hold a winning lottery ticket.
bank.why: Comparing manner + clause = the way.

bank.q: The ice on the driveway was ___ than a skating rink.
bank.why: Comparative + than: more slippery than.

bank.q: Which is the freshest simile for a long wait? It felt ___.
opts: as long as a day without bread
bank.a: as long as a day without bread
bank.why: Like forever and like a lifetime are clichés; the other is specific and unexpected.

bank.q: Our son jumped on the trampoline ___ a kernel in a popcorn machine.
bank.why: Like + noun compares two pictures.

opts: The classroom was like a zoo.
The classroom was louder than a zoo.
bank.why: No comparison word: a metaphor. The others are similes.

bank.q: ___ a lighthouse keeps ships off the rocks, so a good editor keeps writers out of trouble.
bank.why: The epic pattern: just as ..., so ...

bank.q: Which sentence is an extended simile? ___
opts: A career is like a canoe trip: you plan, you paddle, and sometimes you portage.
My career is as good as ever.
bank.a: A career is like a canoe trip: you plan, you paddle, and sometimes you portage.
bank.why: The comparison is developed in several steps, all within one picture.

bank.q: The hotel lobby was as cold ___ a meat locker.
bank.why: As + adjective + as.

bank.q: He answered the phone as ___ he were expecting bad news.
bank.why: As if / as though + were: an imagined situation.

bank.q: She ate the soup the ___ you'd eat it in a five-star restaurant.
bank.why: The way + clause compares manner.

bank.q: The waiting room was quieter ___ a snowy field at midnight.
bank.why: Comparative + than: a fresh simile.

bank.q: Just as rivers find their way to the sea, ___ gossip finds its way to the staff room.
bank.why: Epic simile pattern: just as ..., so ...

bank.q: The baby slept as peaceful like an old dog by the fire.
bank.why: As + adjective + as.

bank.q: The house was more empty as a church on Monday.
bank.why: Comparatives take than: emptier than.

bank.q: He guarded the remote control the way a goalie guards the net.
bank.why: Correct! The way + clause: a fresh simile about manner.

bank.q: The old dog greeted us as if we had been away for a year.
bank.why: Correct! As if + past perfect: an imagined situation.

bank.a: She smiled as if nothing had happened
bank.why: As if + clause: compares with an imagined situation.

bank.a: The office was quieter than a library on Sunday
bank.why: Comparative + than + a fresh, specific picture.

bank.a: He drives the way my grandmother knits
bank.why: The way + clause: slowly and carefully, or skilfully, depending on Grandma.
